# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR)
Description: The Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report is the U.S. government’s only Principal Federal Economic Indicator that provides weekly data; other indicators report either monthly or quarterly data. WNGSR reports the underground working natural gas storage level as of the previous Friday, weekly net change, comparisons to historical levels and net changes, and statistical measures for each of five regions in the Lower 48 states.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report comprehensively. Let me start with several targeted searches.I have solid foundational information. Let me gather more on users, market impact, and data access formats.One more round of searches to confirm the region definitions, OMB designation details, and data stewardship context.# Research Report: Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR)

## Executive Summary & Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate and verifiable**. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) itself states in a *Today in Energy* article (December 2023) that "The Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report (WNGSR) is the U.S. government's only Principal Federal Economic Indicator that provides weekly data; other indicators report either monthly or quarterly data." The rest of your description—data as of the previous Friday, weekly net change, historical comparisons, and five Lower 48 regions—matches the report's published structure exactly.

---

## 1. Publisher and Producing Organization

- **Publisher:** U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), the independent statistical and analytical agency within the **U.S. Department of Energy (DOE)**. EIA has statutory independence: its data and analyses are not subject to clearance or approval by any other DOE or executive-branch official before release.
- **Responsible office:** EIA's Office of Energy Statistics, specifically the natural gas survey program that also runs Forms EIA-191 (monthly), EIA-176, and related surveys.
- **Location:** 1000 Independence Ave., SW, Washington, DC 20585.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Statutory authority for data collection:** Section 13(b) of the **Federal Energy Administration Act of 1974 (Public Law 93-275, 15 U.S.C. 790a)**, as amended. Reporting on Form EIA-912 is **mandatory** for sampled respondents.
- **Sanctions for noncompliance:** Civil penalties up to $2,750/day per violation; criminal fines up to $5,000/day; courts may issue injunctions compelling compliance (per the form instructions filed with OMB).
- **Organizational authority:** EIA itself was created by the **Department of Energy Organization Act of 1977 (P.L. 95-91)**.
- **Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI) status:** The WNGSR is one of roughly three dozen designated PFEIs. PFEIs are governed by **OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3**, which requires a fixed, pre-announced release schedule, strict embargo rules (no advance access except narrowly defined prerelease arrangements), and professional independence. The WNGSR is unique among PFEIs in being weekly.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** Form EIA-912 is cleared under **OMB Control No. 1905-0175** (renewed periodically; the 2018 version listed an estimated respondent burden of 1.0 hour per response). Clearance renewals go through the reginfo.gov public comment process—useful historical records for researchers.

## 3. History and Evolution

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| **1994–2002** | The **American Gas Association (AGA)**, a trade association, first published weekly working gas estimates (three regions: Consuming East, Consuming West, Producing). In October 2001 AGA announced it would discontinue the survey for resource reasons; its last report was May 1, 2002. |
| **2002** | EIA took over the series to preserve this market-critical data. Form **EIA-912** was created; first responses due March 18, 2002 (week ending March 15, 2002). The first full WNGSR release was May 9, 2002 (for week ending May 3, 2002). A November 2002 Federal Register notice established the initial **revision policy**. |
| **1993–2002 backfill** | EIA constructed a *Weekly Historical Estimates Database* back to December 31, 1993 by calibrating AGA weekly data to EIA-191 monthly census data—so the series is not purely survey-based before March 2002. |
| **2005** | A revised estimation methodology took effect (August 4, 2005 release). A new policy for **unscheduled revisions** was set: corrections ≥10 Bcf are released on a federal workday between 2:00–2:10 p.m. ET, after 1:00–1:10 p.m. public notice (70 FR, April 26, 2005). |
| **2012** | EIA began publishing separate **salt vs. nonsalt** breakdowns for the South Central (then Producing) region, backcast to end-2006. Salt caverns cycle rapidly and behave differently from depleted-field/aquifer storage. |
| **2015** | Major redesign: the report moved from **three regions to five** (East, Midwest, South Central, Mountain, Pacific) beginning with the November 19, 2015 release, reflecting shale-era shifts in production geography (e.g., Marcellus). EIA derived a five-region history back to January 2010. The three-region history was archived separately. |
| **2018** | Sample reselection under the five-region design; the **Pacific region became a census** (all eight operators surveyed). Salt/nonsalt reporting for South Central was formalized in the OMB-approved form (late 2017). |
| **2024** | Another sample reselection to reflect changes in the operator population. |

### Region definitions (current)
- **East:** CT, DE, DC, FL, GA, MA, MD, ME, NH, NJ, NY, NC, OH, PA, RI, SC, VT, VA, WV
- **Midwest:** IL, IN, IA, KY, MI, MN, MO, TN, WI
- **Mountain:** AZ, CO, ID, MT, NE, NM, NV, ND, SD, UT, WY
- **Pacific:** CA, OR, WA
- **South Central:** AL, AR, KS, LA, MS, OK, TX (with salt/nonsalt subtotals)

Alaska and Hawaii are excluded ("Lower 48").

## 4. Methodology (Key Points for Data Scientists)

- **Survey instrument:** Form EIA-912, *Weekly Underground Natural Gas Storage Report*. Respondents report working gas volumes as of **9:00 a.m. Central Time Friday**, due to EIA by **5:00 p.m. Eastern the following Monday** (next business day if Monday is a holiday).
- **Sampling design:** A stratified **probability-proportionate-to-size (PPS)** sample drawn from the census frame of Form EIA-191 (Monthly Underground Natural Gas Storage Report), which covers ~133 operators and ~410 storage fields. Six strata: East, Midwest, Mountain, Pacific, South Central Salt, South Central Nonsalt. A **certainty stratum** includes all large and multi-stratum operators. Target: relative standard error ≤5% per stratum; roughly **80–85 respondents** typically covering ≥90–95% of storage capacity per region.
- **Estimation:** Combines the latest EIA-912 weekly reports with 12-month moving averages from EIA-191 monthly data (available on a 60-day lag); weekly behavior of sampled firms within a stratum is used to estimate non-sampled firms.
- **Key definitions:** *Working gas* = gas available for withdrawal (excludes *base/cushion gas*, the permanent inventory needed to maintain reservoir pressure). Volumes reported in MMcf at 14.73 psia, 60°F; published in Bcf.
- **What's measured vs. derived:** "Net change" reflects injections, withdrawals, **and reclassifications** between base and working gas. "Implied flow" adjusts the net change for such reclassifications—an important distinction added to the report.
- **Uncertainty:** EIA publishes estimated measures of sampling variability for the current week's stocks and net changes.

## 5. Release Schedule and Revision Policy

- **Release:** Every **Thursday at 10:30 a.m. Eastern** (shifted for federal holidays; the full-year schedule is published in advance at ir.eia.gov/ngs/schedule.html).
- **Revisions:** Scheduled revisions follow the November 2002 Federal Register policy; a **7 Bcf threshold** triggers note of scheduled revisions, and a **10 Bcf threshold** triggers same-day unscheduled rerelease (with one-hour advance public notice) to avoid market disruption. Reclassifications of base/working gas are *not* treated as revisions—they flow into the next scheduled release, and those exceeding 7 Bcf are flagged in the text.
- **Embargo:** As a PFEI under OMB Directive No. 3, no one gets the data before 10:30 a.m.—this is why the release causes immediate, observable price moves in NYMEX natural gas futures.

## 6. Data Contents and Access

**Each weekly report includes:** working gas stocks (Bcf) by region and Lower 48 total; weekly net change and implied flow; comparison to year-ago levels (% change); comparison to five-year average (% change); position within the five-year range; and sampling-variability estimates.

**Access channels:**
- **HTML report:** https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html
- **Machine-readable CSV of the current report:** https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/wngsr.csv (plus a JSON version)
- **Full history XLS:** https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngshistory.xls (five-region history); archived three-region history at https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/archngshistory.xls
- **EIA Data Browser (dnav):** Weekly Working Gas in Underground Storage table with XLS downloads per region
- **EIA Open Data API v2:** route `natural-gas/stor/wkly` (free API key registration; legacy v1 series IDs such as `NG.NW2_EPG0_SWO_R48_BCF.W` for the Lower 48 total)
- **Related products:** Natural Gas Storage Dashboard (visualization with capacity-utilization context), Natural Gas Weekly Update, and monthly/annual data via Form EIA-191 in the *Natural Gas Monthly*.
- **Cataloged on data.gov** as part of EIA's natural gas storage API dataset.
- **License/terms:** U.S. government work; EIA data are free for public use with attribution.

## 7. Typical Users

- **Commodity traders and financial markets:** This is arguably the single most market-moving weekly energy statistic. NYMEX Henry Hub futures routinely move within seconds of the 10:30 a.m. release when the number deviates from analyst consensus (Reuters/WSJ/Bloomberg surveys publish expected injections/withdrawals beforehand). Financial press coverage treats it as a marquee weekly event.
- **Natural gas producers, marketers, pipelines, and storage operators:** For operational and hedging decisions, basis analysis, and injection/withdrawal planning.
- **Utilities and large consumers:** For supply adequacy and procurement planning, especially ahead of winter.
- **Government and policy:** FERC cites regional storage data in its Energy Primer; EIA itself uses the series in the Short-Term Energy Outlook; regulators and state agencies watch regional tightness (e.g., Pacific region after Aliso Canyon).
- **Academics and data scientists:** Used in energy-economics research on price discovery, volatility, and information efficiency; also a common teaching dataset for time-series work.
- **Journalists and the public:** Seasonal narratives (winter withdrawal season, summer injection season) rely on it.

## 8. Benefits to the Public

1. **Market transparency and efficiency:** A neutral, government-produced benchmark eliminates information asymmetry that existed when only industry (AGA) collected the data. Standardized, simultaneous release prevents insider advantage.
2. **Energy security situational awareness:** Storage is the primary buffer against winter heating demand and summer power-generation peaks; the report shows, weekly, whether the nation is building an adequate cushion.
3. **Regional granularity:** The five-region format (plus salt/nonsalt) reveals localized stress—critical since shale production reconfigured supply flows and regional infrastructure constraints became binding.
4. **Consumer protection and price formation:** Efficient, transparent price discovery in futures markets ultimately flows through to retail gas and electricity rates.
5. **Accountability and statistical standards:** Mandatory reporting with civil/criminal penalties, OMB-cleared methodology, published sampling-error measures, and a formal revision policy make it one of the more rigorously governed commodity statistics in the world.

## 9. Preservation & Data-Stewardship Considerations

For a preservationist, data librarian, or policy activist, the following points matter:

- **Fragility of formats:** The canonical artifacts are an HTML page, a CSV that **overwrites weekly** (wngsr.csv shows only the current report), and XLS history files. The CSV is not an archive—historical retrieval requires ngshistory.xls, the dnav tables, or the API. Web archiving (e.g., Internet Archive captures of ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html) is the main protection for the report's narrative text, special notices, and reclassification flags.
- **Series breaks and archived versions:** The 2015 three-to-five-region change created a structural break; the archived three-region history (archngshistory.xls) must be preserved alongside the current file. The pre-2002 history is *derived*, not surveyed—document this provenance in any archived copy.
- **Revisions:** Weekly values can be revised. Preservation strategies should snapshot versions (with retrieval timestamps) rather than relying on the live API, which reflects only current values.
- **Documentation to archive with the data:** The methodology page (ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html), sample-change notices (2018, 2024), Federal Register notices (67 FR 68581, Nov. 12, 2002; 70 FR, Apr. 26, 2005), the EIA-912 form and instructions (reginfo.gov/omb.report ICR records under OMB 1905-0175), and the definitions/notes pages.
- **Continuity risk:** The series depends on mandatory survey authority and EIA appropriations. The AGA's 2001 discontinuation of the predecessor survey demonstrates that this data stream has already been interrupted once; EIA's takeover is a case study in government stepping in to preserve a public-good dataset. Advocacy for EIA funding and OMB clearance renewals directly affects this dataset's survival.
- **Dependencies:** The WNGSR estimate depends on the EIA-191 monthly census (sampling frame and estimation inputs) and on demonstrated storage-capacity estimates—preserving one without the other degrades interpretability.

## 10. Caveats and Known Limitations

- **Estimates, not census:** Weekly figures are sample-based (except Pacific since 2018); monthly EIA-191 census numbers can differ from end-of-month weekly interpolations (EIA publishes a reconciliation page on these differences).
- **Reclassifications can muddy flows:** Net changes include reclassifications between base and working gas; the "implied flow" column was introduced precisely to address this.
- **Rounding:** Regional components may not sum to the total (independent rounding); the 2015 regional reallocation introduced ±1–2 Bcf differences in derived history.
- **No Alaska/Hawaii; no facility-level data:** Public data are regional aggregates; facility-level data from EIA-191 are published separately in aggregated form, and respondent-level data are confidential.

## Key Sources

- EIA, WNGSR methodology: https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/methodology.html
- EIA, WNGSR report and schedule: https://ir.eia.gov/ngs/ngs.html; /schedule.html
- EIA, *Today in Energy*: "EIA's weekly natural gas products provide timely natural gas data" (Dec. 2023); "New classifications of natural gas storage regions" (Nov. 2015)
- Federal Register: 67 FR 68581 (Nov. 12, 2002, revision policy); 70 FR (Apr. 26, 2005, unscheduled revision policy); Vol. 67 No. 133 (July 11, 2002, WNGSR establishment)
- OMB/reginfo.gov ICR records for Form EIA-912, OMB No. 1905-0175
- EIA Data Browser table definitions: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/ng/TblDefs/ng_stor_wkly_tbldef2.asp
- EIA Open Data API documentation: https://www.eia.gov/opendata/
- FERC Energy Primer (2020) — regional storage capacity context
- EIA Natural Gas Storage Dashboard notes: https://www.eia.gov/naturalgas/storage/dashboard-content/notes_sources.php

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding

### Data Quality

- **Evidence for High Risk:** None. No reduction in granularity, timeliness, or frequency has occurred for WNGSR. The October 8, 2026 release contains the complete structure: five regions, salt/nonsalt South Central subtotals, implied flows, historical comparisons, and estimated measures of sampling variability.
- **Evidence for Moderate Risk:** Agency-wide capacity has eroded: ~30–40% staff loss; documented delays in related natural gas products (the annual *Underground Natural Gas Working Storage Capacity* report was delayed in 2025, per the American Statistical Association's *The Nation's Data at Risk* report); EIA told Reuters it was "reviewing which reports it might have to stop" (April 2025); internal emails described an "all-hands-on-deck" effort to preserve institutional knowledge before further departures. ### Statutory Context

- **Evidence for No Known Issue:** Collection authority is explicit and named on the form: Section 13(b) of the Federal Energy Administration Act of 1974 (15 U.S.C. 790a), mandatory reporting with civil/criminal penalties. WNGSR is a designated Principal Federal Economic Indicator governed by OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3. There is no true alternative data collection — the predecessor AGA survey was discontinued in 2002 and commercial estimates are not substitutes for the official series.
- **Evidence for Moderate Risk:** The statute authorizes EIA's energy data collections broadly but does **not explicitly require** a weekly natural gas storage series — the weekly frequency, sample design, and the report itself exist by agency discretion under that general authority. EIA demonstrated in 2025 that it will discontinue surveys under this same authority when it judges burden exceeds value (solar PV shipments). The series is required for functioning of federal market-transparency and regulatory functions (FERC, DOE emergency planning) and has no substitute — matching the rubric's Moderate definition.
- **Evidence for High Risk:** Partial — authorization is broad rather than specific, but programmatic use is strong and no substitute exists, so the full High-risk profile does not fit.

**→ Moderate Risk.** Explicitly authorized but not explicitly mandated; the report's existence at weekly frequency is discretionary, and 2025 proved that discretionary EIA surveys can be canceled. Strong programmatic use and the absence of substitutes keep it from High.

- **Evidence for No Known Issue:** Only on the budget dimension (flat funding, no cut); contradicted on staffing.

**→ Moderate Risk.** Best-documented staff losses (~29–30%+ of agency staff, 107 FTE reduction projected) sit at the top of the Moderate band; if the full ~40% of buyout acceptances is counted, the situation crosses into the rubric's High definition. ### Policy

- **Evidence for High Risk:** None specific to WNGSR. The EIA-912 ICR is a routine, mandatory collection renewed through 2027 — not a Presidential-Action-driven ICR. The live report page (checked October 9, 2026) carries no negative policy note or banner. No changes to WNGSR have been made in accordance with administration priorities; if anything, weekly natural gas data aligns with the administration's fossil-energy emphasis, and the new Administrator has praised U.S. natural gas prominence.
- **Evidence for Moderate Risk:** EIA leadership told Reuters it was reviewing which reports to discontinue (April 2025) — a general, not WNGSR-specific, signal. The administration attacked EIA's AEO2025 findings in a same-day DOE press release and the AEO narrative was deleted — evidence of political pressure on EIA products broadly, though on analysis products, not this statistical survey. Abbey's confirmation testimony called EIA "in urgent need of revitalization," implying planned changes, though none directed at WNGSR.
- **Evidence for No Known Issue:** Since January 2025, nothing has changed about what WNGSR collects or publishes; the only adjacent change (Natural Gas Weekly Update's retirement, January 2026) came with a new WNGSR Supplement that preserves and consolidates the content around this report. WNGSR survived the shutdown prioritized as an essential/continuing product.

**→ No Known Issue** (with monitoring note). For this dataset specifically, no policy-driven alteration has occurred or been proposed. The agency-wide environment — politicized criticism of EIA outputs, discretionary report cancellations, a leadership "revitalization" agenda — warrants continued monitoring but has not touched WNGSR, whose market-critical, fossil-fuel-oriented, PFEI-designated status appears to shield it.
